1.pericope_label: Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that dwellest between the cherubims, shine forth

schools.summary: Augustine expounds the Greek heading clause by clause and turns its reference to the Assyrian into a moral category by etymology, since the name is interpreted as men guiding, so that the psalm addresses a generation guiding rather than one that has not guided its heart; he reads the whole as a song of the Advent and of the vineyard, of head and body, king and people.

Calvin holds the psalm composed on behalf of the ten tribes after that kingdom began to be wasted, and finds the naming of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh significant for that reason, his block carrying a later explanation from the wilderness marching order; Gill reads the Shepherd throughout as the Messiah and gives the same marching order.

Spurgeon takes the title of Shepherd as chosen for its tenderness, since broken hearts delight in names of grace, and refers it to the dying words of the patriarch; Henry makes the mercy-seat between the cherubim a throne of grace which is such to us only because of the great propitiation, and commits the sheep to the great and good Shepherd.

Clarke reports a view that the three tribes simply stand for the whole nation, states the psalm’s architecture as four parts of which three close with the same refrain, notes an old Cambridge manuscript that writes this psalm and the preceding one as one, and dismisses twenty quarto pages of a Hebrew lexicon on the cherubim as a long and painful system of conjectures; Wesley gives the marching order behind the naming of the tribes.

Ellicott distributes the patriarchal names for God and observes that shepherd and rock belonged especially to one of them, argues from the preposition before that the ancient marching arrangement and no recent political event determines the naming of the tribes, doubts any reference to the northern kingdom, and insists the throne between the cherubim is drawn from the sculptured wings above the ark rather than from clouds; Keil and Delitzsch treat the Greek heading’s reference to the Assyrian as an ancient note that solves the riddle of the tribes.

debates: Why are Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh named? Calvin holds the psalm written for the ten tribes and finds their naming significant of that; the paragraph attached to his block explains it instead from the order of the march in the wilderness, where those three followed immediately behind the ark, and Gill and Wesley give the same; Ellicott presses that explanation into an argument, that the preposition before shows the ancient arrangement and no recent political event to be in view, and doubts any reference to the northern kingdom at all; Clarke reports a fourth view in which the three simply stand for the whole nation.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch treat the Greek heading’s note about the Assyrian as an ancient interpretation that solves the riddle of the tribes, and Augustine is found expounding that very heading clause by clause, turning the same name into a moral category by its etymology.
Clarke states the psalm’s architecture as four parts, three of which close with the same refrain and the fourth with words nearly the same.
Clarke dismisses about twenty quarto pages on the cherubim in a Hebrew lexicon of his day as a long and painful account, or system of conjectures.
Clarke notes an old manuscript at Cambridge that writes this psalm and the one before it as a single psalm.
themes: a heading in the versions used as historical evidence
tribes named by an old order of march
a political reading resisted on grammatical grounds
a throne located in the furniture of a sanctuary
a psalm built on a returning refrain

4.pericope_label: How long wilt thou be angry against the prayer of thy people? thou feedest them with the bread of tears

schools.summary: Spurgeon asks how long the smoke of God’s wrath shall drown the smoking incense of prayer, observes that anger against praying is a bitterer grief than anger against sinning, and turns the bread of tears into meals once merry and now like funeral feasts to which each man brings his bitter morsel.

Gill gives two senses of the bread of tears, tears in the place of bread or bread dipped in them, offers two senses of being made a strife, either being forced to contend for their own defence or their captors quarrelling over the spoil, and notes that the repeated refrain shows what was uppermost in the people’s minds.

Clarke renders the disputed measure threefold and reports both a particular vessel of unknown capacity and a general sense of abundance, and offers as the first sense of the strife that the neighbouring peoples have a controversy about a nation so wonderfully preserved and so wonderfully punished, seeing in it both the goodness and the severity of God.

Ellicott derives the verb from fuming and finds a pregnant construction combining two clauses, reads the preposition as during rather than against the prayer and pictures the smoke of anger as a cloud through which the incense of petition cannot rise, traces the measure to a third part while holding it used generally as we say a peck of troubles, and admits only one sense of being a strife; Keil and Delitzsch mark the strophe as the point where complaint becomes detailed by contrast with former days.

debates: In what sense are they a strife to their neighbours? Gill offers either that they must contend for their own defence or that their captors quarrel among themselves over the spoil; Clarke offers first that the neighbouring peoples have a controversy about a nation so wonderfully preserved and so wonderfully punished, in whom they see both the goodness and the severity of God, and second that all of them join to malign and execrate it; Ellicott admits only the sense of being an object of contention, holding that in no other could the nation be a strife to its neighbours.

What measure of tears is meant? Clarke renders the word threefold and reports that some take it for a particular vessel used by the captors, of unknown capacity, and others for abundance simply; Ellicott derives it from a third part and suggests a third of a standard measure, but holds it used here generally, as we might speak of a peck of troubles.
outliers: Spurgeon and Ellicott independently picture the divine anger and the people’s prayer as two smokes contending, the one a cloud that the ascending incense of the other cannot penetrate.
Spurgeon turns the bread of tears into meals once seasons of social merriment and now like funeral feasts, to which each man contributes his bitter morsel.
Ellicott notes that the enemies laugh literally for themselves, though the older versions make them laugh at us.
themes: wrath described as obstructing prayer rather than punishing sin
sorrow measured out as food and drink
an unknown unit read as a third, a vessel and a heap
a nation made the subject of its neighbours’ quarrel
a refrain marking what the petitioners want most

8.pericope_label: Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: why hast thou then broken down her hedges?

schools.summary: Spurgeon has seven nations digged out to make space and the old trees that engrossed the soil torn up root and branch, and holds the vine chosen though small, dependent and apt to trail on the ground; Henry draws the character of the plant as weak and unsightly yet spreading and fruitful, makes Christ the root and believers the branches, and has the nations swept away as dirt with the besom of destruction.

Gill notes the paradox that the vine grew the more it was afflicted in its first country, names the hedge as the angels that encamp about God’s people and salvation as walls and bulwarks, and reports three identifications of the boar, the Assyrian king who carried the ten tribes away, a later persecutor on one scholar’s reading, and the fourth beast meaning the Roman empire on the Jewish interpreters’.

Clarke catalogues the prophets who use the figure and runs the horticulture as a numbered allegory across five verses, from the transplanting into better soil through the clearing, digging, propping and layering to the fencing that the psalm asks why God has broken down, closing with the note that vines are propagated by layers, seed, grafting and inoculation as well as by cuttings; Wesley takes the sea and river as the limits of the land.

Ellicott guesses the prophetic song of the vineyard to be the parent image unless the patriarchal blessing on Joseph suggested it, takes the opening verb as a historic present and notes that it serves both for horticulture and for striking a nomadic camp, renders the ninth verse as striking its roots deep, and observes that the goodly cedars are literally cedars of God; Keil and Delitzsch likewise trace the figure to the patriarchal blessing where Joseph is a layer whose shoots climb a wall.

debates: What is the boar out of the wood? Gill reports three identifications in one note, the Assyrian king who carried the ten tribes into captivity, for which he cites the Greek heading that assigns the psalm to the Assyrian; a later persecutor of the second century, on one scholar’s reading of the psalm’s date; and the fourth beast, meaning the Roman empire, on the reading of the Jewish interpreters.
outliers: Clarke runs the vine allegory as seven numbered stages of practical viticulture across five verses, from transplanting and clearing to layering and fencing, and ends by noting that vines are propagated by layers, seed, grafting and inoculation as well as by cuttings.
Ellicott observes that the verb for bringing the vine out serves both for horticulture and for breaking up a nomadic encampment, pulling out the tent-pins and driving them in elsewhere.
Clarke notes that under such vines men not only sheltered from the heat but ate, drank and dwelt.
Gill notes the paradox that the vine grew and multiplied the more it was afflicted in the country it was brought out of.
themes: a national history told as the life of one plant
a figure traced back to its earliest user
one verb for transplanting and for striking camp
protection described as a hedge that was removed
a single beast identified with three empires

14.pericope_label: Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: let thy hand be upon the man of thy right hand

schools.summary: Henry makes the man of God’s right hand the Messiah and the arm of the Lord, in whom is the strength by which his people persevere, and concludes that the vine cannot be ruined nor any fruitful branch perish, though the unfruitful will be cut off.

Gill collects five proposals for the word that occurs only here, notes its enlarged and crooked initial letter in the copies and calls it an Egyptian word for a plant, reports three candidates for the man of the right hand and prefers the Messiah on Jewish authority, and notices that the refrain grows as it returns, some finding the Trinity in its three ascending titles.

Clarke argues the messianic reading from the text itself, citing an Aramaic version that renders the phrase the King Messiah, five ancient versions and eighteen manuscripts reading son of man, and concludes that this is the first place in the older scriptures where that title is applied to Christ, adding that an old English psalter understood it of his session at God’s right hand; he also observes that the Jews were never guilty of idolatry after the captivity. Wesley takes the son of man for the people, spoken of as one person.

Ellicott reports that most modern scholars make the word rendered vineyard the imperative of a verb meaning protect, rearranges the closing section so that the verse about burning follows the verse about the beasts and the verse about the man of the right hand follows the verse about the vineyard, and denies the messianic reading, holding that parallelism and context show the poet to be thinking of the nation as a community.

debates: Who is the man of thy right hand? Clarke argues from an Aramaic version rendering it the King Messiah, from five ancient versions and eighteen manuscripts reading son of man, and from the impossibility of anyone else standing at God’s right hand as intercessor, and concludes that this is the first place in the older scriptures where that title is applied to Christ; Gill reports the people, the reigning king and the Messiah as candidates and prefers the last on Jewish authority; Henry agrees. Ellicott denies it, holding that parallelism and context show the poet to be thinking of the nation as a community of which the vine is the emblem, and Wesley takes the same side.

What is the word that occurs only here? Gill reports it rendered a branch or shoot, a plant, a habitation, and as an adjective meaning established, and himself calls it an Egyptian word for a plant; Ellicott reports that most modern scholars follow the two oldest versions in making it the imperative of a verb meaning protect, which yields a better parallelism.
outliers: Ellicott rearranges the closing section on grounds of sense and rhythm, moving the verse about burning to follow the verse about the beasts, so that it is the beasts and not the people who perish at God’s rebuke, and moving the verse about the man of the right hand to follow the verse about the vineyard.

Gill notes that the initial letter of the word occurring only here is written larger than usual in the copies, which some take as a memorial of the vine’s coming out of Egypt, its crooked shape hinting at the vine’s later oppression.
Gill observes that the refrain grows each time it returns, addressing first God, then the God of hosts, then the Lord God of hosts, and reports that some have found the Trinity suggested there.
themes: a word used once and understood five ways
verses moved to make the sense and the rhythm agree
a title claimed as its own first appearance
a nation and a person contending for one phrase
a refrain that lengthens as the psalm proceeds
